sources.title: NASA’s Space X CRS-35 Launch Jellyfish

items.title: Why a Launch Near Dawn Leaves a Jellyfish in the Sky
items.body: A rocket can leave a sky-sized jellyfish behind it. A SpaceX Falcon 9 carrying a Dragon spacecraft lifted off on Oct. 13, 2026, and NASA photographed the exhaust plumes glowing in the shape the agency calls a jellyfish. The mechanism is sunlight, not chemistry: NASA says the effect happens near sunrise or sunset, when the plume from the rocket is brightly illuminated and takes on a jellyfish-like glow. Timing does the work — the exhaust has to be up there at the one part of the day when light is arriving at that angle. This particular launch left the pad at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, carrying scientific investigations, supplies and equipment toward the International Space Station. It is a reminder that some of the best launch photography is not about the rocket at all, but about where the Sun happens to be standing.

sources.title: Schools across US protest FCC plan that could disconnect kids from Internet

discussion.body: Two arguments are being fused here. Whether districts overdid screen time is one question; whether a connectivity subsidy should exist at all is another. The chairman's complaint answers the first and leans on it for the second.

Separable in theory, tangled in practice: the districts defending E-Rate are the same districts being accused of overreach, so the politics will run on both tracks whether or not the policy logic does.

Keep the instrument in view, though. This is a discount program for telecom services and equipment, not a curriculum mandate. Cutting it changes what a library can buy more reliably than it changes what a teacher assigns.

items.title: Schools Ask the FCC to Spare E-Rate, a $2 Billion-a-Year Internet Subsidy
items.body: Schools and libraries around the United States have pleaded with the Federal Communications Commission to drop the idea of ending E-Rate, the program worth about $2 billion a year that connects students and library visitors to the internet. The pushback comes after FCC Chairman Brendan Carr criticized school districts for having, in his words, experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students, and argued that E-Rate had expanded too far beyond its original purpose of supporting basic internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes. In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be limited or sunset to reflect today's extensive connectivity rates. His proposal could result in the program cutting the discounts schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. Because the agency is also taking comment on whether to sunset the program, the possibility that Carr could axe E-Rate entirely is live.

sources.title: MK2 Films Scores Brady Corbet, Kleber Mendonça Filho, Céline Sciamma Shorts (EXCLUSIVE)

items.title: MK2 Picks Up Shorts by Corbet, Mendonça Filho and Sciamma
items.body: Short films by Brady Corbet, Kleber Mendonça Filho and Céline Sciamma are joining the international sales catalogue of MK2 Films. Variety reports that the Paris-based company is expanding its collection of lesser-seen works by established filmmakers, and that the acquisitions were unveiled during Lyon's Lumière Film Festival — headed by Cannes director Thierry Frémaux — and its International Classic Film Market. It reads as a bet on name recognition over running time: a short by a director with a following can travel through a sales catalogue in a way an anonymous short generally cannot, and a festival market built around classic and archival cinema is a natural place to announce it. The interesting question is whether the catalogue treatment turns shorts into something bookable rather than merely awardable.

sources.title: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations

items.title: Ukraine's Pentagon-Funded Starshield Network Was Partly Disabled
items.body: A key component of Ukraine's communications network was partially disabled on Wednesday. PBS NewsHour reports that the Starshield satellite network — funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX — was not operating at full capacity, hampering communications within the Ukrainian military. The reporting describes a degradation rather than a clean outage, but for an army that runs much of its coordination through satellite links, partial capacity is the kind of condition that shows up first in the units least able to route around it. The arrangement itself is worth noticing: a capability paid for by the US Defense Department and run by a commercial company, which puts a private operator in the chain between a government's money and a battlefield's connectivity. Anchor Amna Nawaz discussed the developments with retired US Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery.

sources.title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation

discussion.body: DAVINCI is only the opening move. NASA's second mission, VERITAS, is scheduled for a November 2032 launch to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit, and the European Space Agency is building its own orbiter, Envision, also bound for Venus in 2032.

Those two kinds of measurement answer different questions. A radar orbiter produces a map built from returns; a descent probe puts a lens below the clouds. The second is the rarer commodity here, which is why the December 2030 date is the one to remember.

items.title: Venus, by Parachute: DAVINCI Would Return the First Direct Surface Images Since 1982
items.body: Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s, Ars Technica reports, and the first one now has a date. DAVINCI is scheduled for launch in December 2030, and it will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through the planet's atmosphere, returning the first direct images of the Venusian surface since 1982. Be precise about that claim: not the best images since, not the most detailed — the first direct ones at all in that stretch. The 1982 date is doing the heavy lifting in the story, because it marks how long the planet has gone without a close-up look at the ground. If the schedule holds, the next one arrives 48 years later.

sources.title: ‘Lupin’ Star Omar Sy Voices Support For French High School Protests; Decries Authoritarian Response

items.title: Omar Sy Backs France's High School Protests and Faults the Crackdown
items.body: The French star Omar Sy has voiced support for the high school student protests sweeping France and decried the authoritarian crackdown, Deadline reports — a crackdown the outlet says has seen one teenager lose a hand and more than 6,000 young people taken into temporary police custody. According to Deadline, the protests have been building since late September and were sparked by complaints of staff shortages and dilapidated schools. A celebrity endorsement does not change the underlying grievance, but it changes who hears about it. Sy's audience is global and largely tuned to entertainment rather than French domestic politics, which makes his intervention one of the few ways the dispute travels beyond the country's own news cycle.

sources.title: Skydance Shares Tumble In Technical Adjustment As Inflation, Interest Rate Jitters Roil Markets; Apple Regains $5 Trillion Market Cap

items.title: Skydance Shares Fell 22% After Warrants Went Out; Inflation Dragged the Wider Market
items.body: Deadline reports that Skydance shares closed down 22% on Wednesday, ending the session at just over $7, after the company distributed warrants to investors. The same day carried a broader story: Apple shares rose, but tech stocks and overall markets mostly ended in the red after a worse-than-expected September inflation reading sparked fears of higher interest rates, with the pressure landing especially hard on debt-heavy companies, according to Deadline. It is worth keeping the two movements apart. A 22% single-session fall invites the reading that something went wrong inside the business; the reported trigger here is a corporate distribution of warrants, while the day's general weakness is attributed to inflation and rate expectations. Those are different pieces of machinery, even when they show up in the same headline.

sources.title: Thousands of NI workers to get pay bump as Real Living Wage rises

items.title: The Real Living Wage Is a Rate Employers Opt Into — and About 6,000 Workers in Northern Ireland Are Paid It
items.body: The Real Living Wage is not imposed on employers. It is a rate they pay voluntarily, set to reflect the cost of living, and the BBC reports that about 6,000 workers in Northern Ireland are paid it. The word doing the work in that sentence is voluntarily. A wage floor that employers choose to adopt reaches only as far as employers choose to adopt it, so the number of workers covered is itself the measure of the idea's spread. In Northern Ireland, that measure is roughly 6,000 people — small enough that the rate's influence depends less on the figure it sets than on how many employers decide the figure is worth paying.

sources.title: ‘Beach Fictions’ Review: Utterly Beguiling, Time-Tweaking Korean Romance Shows What a Day a Difference Makes

discussion.body: The premise is the argument. If both versions of the day are plausible, the film can weigh fatalism against self-determination without settling it, because neither branch is the correction of the other.
Or the doubled day is just a showcase for the actress playing both branches. The review's own word for the fight is “gently” — nothing here suggests the film picks a winner.

items.title: A Korean Romance Runs the Same Day Twice
items.body: Variety's review of “Beach Fictions” describes it as a diptych that follows one young woman through two diverging versions of the same day. The critic calls it enchanting and subtly profound, and frames the two branches as a contest: fatalism, self-determination and imagination all gently wrestling for control of the narrative — or narratives. What the film is after, in the review's reading, is the question of which voices, inner and otherwise, we grant the most control in our lives. That is a structural idea, not a twist: the same hours, run twice, with the divergence doing the arguing.

items.title: EU Leaders Meet on China Trade and the Next Budget
items.body: EU leaders gathering in Brussels will examine measures to curb what Deutsche Welle calls the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. They will also be looking to move toward agreement on the next EU budget, with major elections coming next year — the two files sharing one summit agenda rather than one priority.

sources.title: After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back

items.title: Few Details on How Hundreds of Thousands Lost ACA Coverage, as the Effort's Next Stage Begins
items.body: The Trump administration canceled hundreds of thousands of Affordable Care Act enrollments while providing few details about the process it used, NPR reports — and the next stage of the anti-fraud effort is already under way. That ordering is the part worth sitting with. The cancellations are large enough to count as a coverage event, but a process the administration has not described is a process that cannot be checked from outside it. And because a further phase of the effort is running now, the questions that follow from the first phase — what put a person on the list, and how they would find out — are being asked after the decisions rather than before them.

sources.title: Netflix Is Finally Reporting Box Office Data. Why Is It Starting with ‘La Bola Negra’?

discussion.body: Four screens is a hedge as much as a test — small enough that a soft result can be waved off as a platform release behaving like one, small enough that a strong per-screen average becomes a clean headline.
The hedge is the point. You find out whether your numbers travel on a title you aren't betting the year on, and only then spend on the ones you are. That's what the test balloon is for.

items.title: Netflix's Awards Hopeful Gets Four Screens First, as a Test Balloon
items.body: The streamer's awards hopeful opens in limited release on four screens this weekend, IndieWire reports — a deliberately small footprint described as a test balloon before the company tries to make a splash with “Cliff Booth” and “Narnia.” Four screens cannot produce a meaningful gross. They can produce a per-screen average, which is the number that circulates when a platform release is going well, and they give the streamer a rehearsal for reporting on a title it is not betting the year on. Note the sequence IndieWire lays out: the small run first, the bigger swings later.

sources.title: SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours

items.title: OpenAI Says Daybreak Cut SentinelOne's Malware Analysis From Weeks to Hours
items.body: OpenAI says its Daybreak tool helped SentinelOne cut malware analysis from weeks to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats. Both the compression of weeks into hours and the resulting extra capacity arrive as the company's own account of a customer deployment — a vendor case study rather than an outside evaluation. The capacity half is the one to hold onto. A speed figure says one task finishes faster; a capacity figure says the team now does more of something than it used to. If the second claim holds up, it would change what gets looked at, not only how long a single analysis takes.

sources.title: For some Christians, Hegseth's plan for public execution fits a biblical mandate

items.title: A Livestreamed Execution Drew Condemnation — and NPR Reports It Isn't an Outlier in Hegseth's Church
items.body: Defense Secretary Hegseth's announcement of a livestreamed execution drew disgust and condemnation from some faith leaders and politicians, NPR reports. NPR also reports that within his church, the position is not an outlier. Put those together and the reaction reads less like a believers-versus-nonbelievers story than a disagreement inside American Christianity. The condemnation is real and it is loud; the reporting simply places Hegseth's own religious community somewhere other than in the chorus.

sources.title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream

items.title: 72 Former Officers Argue That Livestreaming an Execution Would Stain the Military's Honor
items.body: Seventy-two former officers signed a letter arguing against putting Nidal Hasan's execution on a livestream, the BBC reports. Their words: the broadcast “will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it.” The phrasing is the story. The signatories object to the cameras rather than the sentence, which makes this a narrower and, for the Pentagon, more awkward argument than a general objection to capital punishment. It says the injury from an execution watched live lands on the institution and the country — on the people who carry it out and the public that tunes in — not only on the man being put to death. Institutions usually answer that kind of claim with procedure. Here the claim is about reputation, and reputation is harder to litigate.

sources.title: ‘Whalefall’ Review: Austin Abrams Battles a Bellyful of Daddy Issues in Brutal Survival Thriller

discussion.body: “Nearly sink” is doing a lot of work there. It implies the film survives its own baggage, which is more generous than saying the two halves fight each other to a draw.

Or the baggage is the point of calling it a sincere adaptation — a faithful version of the novel has to carry the interiority, and a critic can respect that while still noticing where the balance tips.

items.title: ‘Whalefall’: Exceptional Underwater Body Horror, Nearly Sunk by Its Own Baggage
items.body: IndieWire's review credits Brian Duffield with “exceptional underwater body horror” in a “sincere adaptation” of Daniel Kraus's novel, then adds the dagger: the film “packs enough emotional baggage to nearly sink its ingenious premise.” That is a compliment and a diagnosis in one sentence. Survival thrillers run on the ruthlessness of their premise; an adaptation also has to drag a novel's interior life into that container. Read the metaphor closely and the emotional material is treated as cargo — weight the premise has to float — rather than fuel for it. The hedge matters too. “Nearly sink” leaves the thing afloat, which is a different verdict from a pan, and a more interesting one: a film that works in its set pieces and wobbles when it stops to grieve. Whether you find that wobble moving or tiresome probably depends on how much catharsis you want with your claustrophobia.

sources.title: Want to go as Angine de Poitrine for Halloween? You're in luck

discussion.body: The couples version is the better product design in any case: two buyers, one decision, and someone else has to sign off on the joke before the money moves.
But that's also the risk. A single costume is an independent choice; a coordinated one is a joint decision, and joint decisions are where most Halloween plans quietly die in October.

items.title: A Couple’s Costume for a Couple Hundred Bucks, and What That Price Is Really Buying
items.body: CBC reports that for a couple hundred dollars, you and a partner can buy an Angine de Poitrine couples costume from Party Expert, one of Canada's biggest party supply stores — pitched as an option for anyone tired of dressing up as salt-and-pepper shakers. Consider the genre. A couples costume is a coordination problem before it's a purchase: two people have to agree on the reference, and both have to want the bit more than they want to look normal in the group photo. Salt-and-pepper shakers are the safe floor, legible in any room with no in-joke required. A very specific reference inverts that entirely — its value is the moment someone recognises it. Two hundred dollars is a wager on your guest list, which is bold, and the kind of bold that only works if your partner is in on the joke.

sources.title: Kenora residents applaud ‘fantastic’ move to permanent daylight time

items.title: Northwestern Ontario's Clock Rule Now Runs Along the 90th Meridian
items.body: The provincial government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian will stop the twice-annual clock change. The cutoff is a line of longitude rather than a list of towns, which makes the rule easy to state and strange to live beside: in this corner of the province, whether your clocks get moved twice a year is settled by how far west you are, not by which municipality you belong to. Communities on the western side of that line are to hold one time setting year-round instead of shifting twice a year.
